The regulator’s October 2026 fact sheet showed that imports by oil marketing companies and the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited averaged 15 million litres per day in October, against 28.9 million litres in October 2025.
Also, consumption, measured by volumes trucked out to the domestic market, was 46.5 million litres daily, down from 56.7 million litres a year earlier. However, both figures rose on a monthly basis.
Imports increased 47 per cent from 10.2 million litres daily in September, while consumption rose five per cent from 44.4 million litres.
Total petrol receipts rose 21 per cent in October to 46.9 million litres daily from 38.7 million litres in September. Domestic refineries supplied 31.9 million litres, up 12 per cent. Local refineries supplied about 68 per cent of receipts, against about 37 per cent in October 2025, when they provided 17.1 million litres of 46 million litres received.
Supply remained below the 50 million litres per day demand benchmark and the 13-month average of 50.2 million litres. Imports were below their 13-month average of 18.8 million litres daily and well under the 52.1 million litres recorded in November 2025, the highest in the period.
The fact sheet showed that consumption was 93 per cent of the benchmark and below the 13-month mean of 51 million litres. It peaked at 63.7 million litres daily in December 2025.
The Authority said higher crude receipts at domestic refineries and strong local petrol supply from the Dangote refinery meant most of the petrol consumed in October was refined in Nigeria. It said this reduced reliance on imports, eased pressure on foreign exchange and improved supply security.
The Dangote refinery produced 48.51 million litres of petrol daily and ran at 103.73 per cent of its 650,000 barrels per day capacity, down 2.25 percentage points from September. Of its petrol output, 31.89 million litres went to the domestic market and 20.18 million litres, or 42 per cent of production, was exported. It drew 3.56 million litres daily from stock, and closing petrol stock fell 37 per cent to 229.9 million litres.
Crude receipts at domestic refineries rose 19 per cent to 0.736 million barrels per day. Imported crude to Dangote grew 39 per cent to 118.4 thousand barrels per day, lowering the local crude share to 83.9 per cent from 86.1 per cent.
The Port Harcourt, Warri and Kaduna refineries were not producing. Among modular refineries, Edo ran at 114.89 per cent of capacity, WalterSmith at 58.10 per cent, Aradel at 30.93 per cent and OPAC at 24.86 per cent. Duport was shut down. The modular refineries supplied 0.68 million litres of diesel daily, about 4.9 per cent of the 14 million litres benchmark.
Petrol stock cover fell to 21.8 days from 23.9 days in September, 8.2 days below the required 30-day threshold. Inland depots held 19.53 days and vessels offshore 2.28 days. LPG cover was lower at 14.8 days. Diesel cover was 43.9 days and aviation fuel 75.8 days, both above the threshold.
Diesel supply nearly doubled, rising 93 per cent to 16.8 million litres daily from 8.7 million litres. Imports rose to 6.1 million litres from 0.6 million litres, and domestic supply grew 32 per cent to 10.7 million litres. Supply moved above the 14 million litres benchmark and consumption of 15.5 million litres.
Aviation fuel supply fell 36 per cent to 2.1 million litres daily, below consumption of 2.8 million litres and the 3 million litres benchmark. It was the lowest since July 2026. The Dangote refinery produced 26.44 million litres of aviation fuel daily, with exports taking 84 per cent. The Authority noted that the stock cover figure includes export-bound Dangote stock of 199.7 million litres.
Cooking gas (LPG) supply rose 11 per cent to 5.2 kilotonnes per day, with domestic sources providing 4.8 kilotonnes. Consumption was 5.0 kilotonnes. Average petrol pump prices across eight monitored states rose about three per cent to N1,416.75 per litre, at the lower end of the indicative range of N1,413.71 to N1,447.00. The lowest actual prices were below the indicative minimum in all eight states.
Cooking gas retailed from N1,208 per kilogramme in Lagos to N1,600 in Bauchi.
Maximum retail prices exceeded the indicative price in all eight states monitored.
Dated Brent crude averaged $124.77 per barrel, up seven per cent from September. Gasoline free-on-board cost fell eight per cent to $1,141.38 per metric tonne. The naira traded at N1,338.54 to the dollar, up one per cent.
Total wholesale gas supply averaged 4.95 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) from January to October 2026. Domestic supply averaged 2.04 bcf/d, or 41.3 per cent, while supply to Nigeria LNG (NLNG) averaged 2.91 bcf/d, or 58.7 per cent.
Supply peaked at 5.14 bcf/d in April and dipped to 4.723 bcf/d in July. In October it was 4.951 bcf/d, up 2.7 per cent on September, with domestic supply at 2.113 bcf/d and NLNG at 2.838 bcf/d.
Gas-to-power rose 10 per cent to 0.571 bcf/d. LNG exports rose seven per cent to 52,721 metric tonnes per day, and pipeline exports via the West African Gas Pipeline rose 11 per cent to 0.149 bcf/d.
Gas processing plants held 16.187 bcf/d of installed capacity across 47 plants and processed 8.401 bcf/d, an average utilisation of 51.90 per cent. Four of the seven major facilities ran above 80 per cent, led by Gbaran Ubie at 90.64 per cent. Three ran below 50 per cent, with OB/OB at 25.69 per cent and Utorogu at 29.41 per cent. Condensate production rose from 1.505 million barrels in January to 2.209 million barrels in October.
The Obiafu-Obrikom-Oben (OB3) pipeline reached 100 per cent completion in October. The Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano pipeline stood at 84.27 per cent after being re-scoped to include additional ancillary works. The Odidi-Warri expansion was at 79.58 per cent, the Escravos-Odidi pipeline at 34.75 per cent and the Escravos-Lagos compressor project at 97.18 per cent.
The Authority said steady receipts remain important for supply stability, with rebuilding stock buffers as the next priority.
